questions.q: Why doesn't a GL_JE_HEADERS row carry a dollar amount by itself?
options: Because journal headers are never used in Oracle Financials
Because dollar amounts are stored only in GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS
Because GL_JE_HEADERS is a view, not a real table
Because the actual debit/credit amounts live on GL_JE_LINES, one row per line
questions.explain: A journal header represents the journal entry as a whole; the individual debit and credit amounts are recorded on GL_JE_LINES.

questions.q: Which column connects GL_JE_LINES to GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS?
questions.explain: GL_JE_LINES.CODE_COMBINATION_ID joins to GL_CODE_COMBINATIONS.CODE_COMBINATION_ID to identify which account each line hits.

questions.q: Why does Financials typically filter journals by accounting period (via GL_PERIODS) rather than a plain calendar date range?
options: GL_PERIODS has no date information at all
Accounting periods don't always align exactly with calendar months, and GL_PERIODS also carries closing status, which matters for close work
Calendar date filtering is not supported in Oracle SQL
questions.explain: Accounting periods (e.g., a 13-period fiscal calendar) may not match calendar months, and GL_PERIODS additionally tracks whether a period is open or closed.

questions.q: In `GL_JE_HEADERS`, which column is used to join to `GL_PERIODS`?
questions.explain: GL_JE_HEADERS.PERIOD_NAME joins to GL_PERIODS.PERIOD_NAME to bring in period start/end dates and closing status.

questions.q: Which three subledger/ledger chains did Chapter 2 build, in order?
options: General Ledger, Fixed Assets, Cash Management
questions.explain: Chapter 2 covered Payables (supplier/invoice/payments), Receivables (customer/transaction/receipts), and General Ledger (journal/lines/periods).
